Suites: ipc-machine-chooser (73), chooser-menu (57), host-settings (65), relay-account, chooser-link-hover (22), chooser-restore-all (31), chooser-restore-all-remote (40), chooser-close-chord (14), chooser-roster-refetch (8) all ALL PASS. Floor: none/win32/agent PASS (161s/213s/223s), P1-P3 ALL PASS (25/20/16), five harness sweeps green. Filed T792 and T793: two PRE-EXISTING red scripts found while sweeping the neighbours - `persistence-flag.ps1` has four launch sites that state no persistence, and `chooser-resume.ps1` fails its setup at HEAD (reproduced with this task's one converted line reverted, so it is neither caused nor masked here).
- 2026-08-12: T746 - Ctrl+Shift+N opens the machine chooser from anywhere in the window, not just from a terminal pane. User report 2026-08-11: the chord "does nothing". It was never a dead keybind - it is not a keybind at all. T22c decision 3 settled that the core has no `new_remote_window` action, so Windows intercepts the chord locally, and "locally" meant one `if` inside `Surface.handleKeyEvent` - reached only while a TERMINAL pane owns the focus. The same keystroke therefore meant three things inside one window: from a terminal it opened the chooser; from a focused VIEWER pane it came back through `viewer_accel`, which forwards BINDING ACTIONS, so the cross-platform `ctrl+shift+n -> new_window` default won and it opened a plain local window; and with the TOP-LEVEL window focused (which is where focus sits after almost any app-created control is destroyed) `Window.wndProc` had no WM_KEYDOWN arm at all and the key was dropped - the literal report. Confirmed against the user's own installed-release log before touching code: `machine chooser: opening via ctrl+shift+n` appears through builds up to ~2026-08-04, and their most recent session opens the chooser `via command surface` only, i.e. the palette fallback somebody reaches for when the chord is dead. New pure `src/apprt/win32/window_chord.zig` is now the ONE definition of a window-scoped chord that has no action to look up (strict about absent modifiers, so alt/win variants stay available to the keybind set); `Surface.handleKeyEvent`, a new `Window.wndProc` WM_KEYDOWN arm and `ViewerPane.claimsChord`/`WM_APP_VIEWER_ACCEL` all consult it, the viewer's check sitting BEFORE the keybind table because that ordering is what the `new_window` default was winning on. `Surface.getModifiers` is `pub` rather than a third copy of the same GetKeyState block. No Mac half is owed: Cmd-Shift-N there is an NSMenu key equivalent, and `performKeyEquivalent` runs ahead of the responder chain, so no focus target can shadow it. New `test\win32\chooser-open-chord.ps1` ALL PASS (10): the three focus states, each also asserting that no plain window appeared instead, with a mandatory terminal-focus positive control first and `-NegativeControl` inverting sections 2 and 3 to the pre-fix expectation (goes red, 2 failures). Its own first run scored two of those window-count assertions VACUOUSLY - PS 5.1 unrolls a one-element array on return, so `.Count` was $null on both sides of the comparison - fixed at the call site and filed as T794 for a sweep of the same shape. Floor green: all three zig lanes PASS, P1-P3 ALL PASS, and the six static harness audits pass except the pre-existing `persistence-flag.ps1` red (T744's four sites, 4 of 179 - this change adds a declared launch, not a violation). Also recorded T747's root cause, found free in the same log: every Sign in press logs `relay account: sign-in failed err=error.NoClientId`, so the button is wired and the shipped build simply carries no Google client id.
- 2026-08-12: T747 - the machine chooser stops offering a Google sign-in button it cannot use. User report 2026-08-11: clicking Sign in with Google does nothing. It was never an unwired button - T746's read of the user's installed-release log had already caught every press logging `relay account: sign-in failed err=error.NoClientId`, i.e. the shipped build carries no `-Dgoogle-client-id` and none is in the environment, so `relay_signin.signIn` returns before it can open a browser. Two separate defects sat behind that one symptom, and only one of them is code: the PRESENTATION of a build with no credential, and the fact that no delivered build has one (the second is T795, gated on decision D72 - only the user has the credential). Mac has never had the presentation hole: `MachineChooserView.accountRow` branches on `RelayAccount.isConfigured` and draws a sentence with NO button (MachineChooserView.swift:1148-1155), while win32's account row knew only three states and drew the enabled button unconditionally - so this is a parity gap, not a new design. `chooser_layout.AccountState` gains `unconfigured` as its fourth member, packing the row with no control at all and the sentence taking the whole band (design system: chrome that controls nothing does not appear), asserted at 1.0/1.25/1.5/2.0; `relay_signin.isConfigured` is the shared resolver Mac's `isConfigured` mirrors; the row says `Google sign-in isn't set up in this build` and the footer hint carries the remedy - both ways to supply an id plus `docs/design/relay-oidc-setup.md` - instead of the old `use Sign in with Google above`, which pointed at a button that is no longer drawn. Deliberately narrow: `unconfigured` replaces only the signed-OUT case, so a stored account is still offered Sign Out (which needs no client id) and an in-flight sign-in still describes itself. `onAccountClicked` refuses the flow as well as the widget hiding it, because a synthesized `BM_CLICK` still reaches a hidden button. WHY IT SHIPPED DEAD is the more useful half: every GUI section of `test\win32\relay-account.ps1` sets `GHOSTTY_GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID=cid-e2e` - a legitimate seam for a fake relay, and also a statement that the unset case is untested. The state every real user meets had never once been exercised, so a dead button read as a fully-tested feature. New section 8 launches without one and asserts the whole presentation, including that a click on the hidden button starts no browser flow and logs no failure, and ends with the identical launch WITH an id as its control, so "no button" cannot pass against a chooser whose account row failed to build. That generalises, and is filed as T796. Two neighbours were red as a direct consequence and are repaired rather than weakened: `chooser-controls.ps1` and `ipc-machine-chooser.ps1` both measure the signed-out button, so both now pin a client id for their launches (their subject is the lookup and the geometry, and which state a build lands in must not depend on whether the box has a `google-client-id.txt`) - and `ipc-machine-chooser`'s null-guard around those measurements became an assertion, since it had been silently skipping two of them. `readDevGoogleClientID` also reads a repo-root `google-client-id.txt` now: the id is baked into the Windows binary too, so a Windows seat should not have to put its build config under `macos/`. Validation: `relay-account.ps1` ALL PASS with section 8 (sections 1-7 unchanged), `chooser-controls.ps1` (46), `ipc-machine-chooser.ps1` (74), plus chooser-menu (57), chooser-sessions (17), chooser-sessions-remote (20), chooser-restore-all (31), chooser-restore-all-remote (40), chooser-open-chord (10), chooser-close-chord (14), chooser-link-hover (22), chrome-theme (64) and host-settings (65) - every script that opens a chooser, since hiding a control changes the Tab cycle. Floor: none/win32/agent PASS via `floor-lane.ps1 -Lane all`, P1-P3 ALL PASS (25/20/16).

- 2026-08-12: T748 - a maximized window that comes back after a restart is actually maximized again, instead of a window Windows still calls maximized sitting at a normal window's size with no border. User report, 2026-08-11: after an upgrade every restored window rendered oddly and had no frame. The mechanism was an ordering one. By the time restore applies a recorded frame the window has already been SHOWN - and shown maximized whenever the T85 placement memory says the user's last window was, which for someone who works maximized is every window on every launch - and `SetWindowPos` moves and resizes a maximized window WITHOUT clearing `WS_MAXIMIZE`. So `IsZoomed` stayed true (caption drops its resize border, chrome lays out for a full-screen window) at the recorded restore-down rect, and the `ShowWindow(SW_MAXIMIZE)` behind it could not undo that: asking for a state the window is already in does nothing. Measured directly before the fix: `restored: 800x600 at 32,32 zoomed=True`. The mirror image was equally broken and is the half nobody had reported - a window the manifest records as NOT maximized, restored while the memory says maximized, kept the maximize style at its small rect. `applyRestoreFrame` now applies both halves with `SetWindowPlacement`, the one call that sets `rcNormalPosition` and the show state together, so no intermediate state exists to be caught in; the pre-show case (a window whose first `ShowWindow` has not happened) still moves with `SetWindowPos` and lets the manifest - not the memory - decide `start_maximized`, and a `GetWindowPlacement` failure falls back to an ORDERED two-step that un-maximizes before it moves. Two things fell out of doing it properly. `WINDOWPLACEMENT.rcNormalPosition` is in workspace coordinates (screen, shifted by the primary work area origin) while the manifest, `restore_frame`'s monitor math and `SetWindowPos` are all in screen coordinates, and the capture side had been storing the raw workspace rect for maximized windows - a taskbar-sized drift on any desktop whose taskbar is at the top or the left, invisible on every other one; both ends now go through the new pure `window_placement.zig` (none lane). And `SW_SHOWNOACTIVATE` through `SetWindowPlacement` DOES clear a maximized state - measured on the box, against what `ShowWindow`'s "most recent size and position" wording suggests - so the un-maximized case keeps the pre-existing no-activation promise instead of having to take the foreground. New acceptance `test\win32\session-restore-maximized.ps1` (ALL PASS, 22) runs both directions with the predicate double-checked: a live-maximized window is the positive control for "fills the screen", and the restored window's `rcNormalPosition` is asserted equal to the manifest's frame, which is what distinguishes a real placement from a call that did nothing to an already-maximized window. Teeth-checked against a binary built from the pre-fix `App.zig`: 3 FAILURE(S) there, ALL PASS here. One harness lesson worth keeping: section B patches the manifest on disk, and writing it with `Set-Content -Encoding UTF8` (PowerShell 5.1 emits a BOM) made the JSON unparseable, restore fell back to "no local manifest", and the fresh window it opened instead looked enough like a restored one to score the section green for the wrong reason.
- 2026-08-12: T745 - a banner table that appeared capped at ~50% of a wide pane was drawing exactly the string it was handed. Reported 2026-08-11 with a screenshot: the pane banner's `Prompt` row stopped near the halfway mark of a ~1900px pane, ending in an ellipsis with the whole right half of the row empty. Reproduced end to end on the test desktop with a window capture, and the renderer came back innocent: fed the same two-row table with the FULL text, the value column ran the entire content width and wrapped; fed the text as the user's banner actually receives it, it stopped at the same halfway mark. The ellipsis is not Ghoztty's tail truncation at all - it is the literal `...` that `~/.claude/scripts/ghoztty-banner.sh`'s `prompt-hook` appends after cutting the auto-seeded prompt to 97 characters, before `+set-banner` is ever called. A cap counted in CHARACTERS cannot know how wide a pane is, so it truncates before the width is used, and on a wide pane 97 characters run out around the middle. `banner_layout.columnWidths` was already correct: on overflow the narrow label column keeps its natural width and every unused pixel goes to the wide value column. The hook's cap is now 400 (a bound on what goes in the per-pane state file, past any width a pane can show), leaving where text stops to the renderer, which word-wraps to the pane's content width and only then ellipsizes at 3 lines. What the repo gained is the measurement that was missing: every T123 oracle in `pane-banner.ps1` 6g is a band HEIGHT, and a column granted only half the pane satisfies all of them - the long value simply wraps one line later - so the suite could not have caught the defect it was reported as. New 6g2 measures the text's own right edge against the content column (chevron reservation excluded, ink threshold 200 so the collapse fade and the elevation shadow cannot pass for text at every x): 96.6% of a 1297px content column on the shipped build, and 33% when rebuilt with `T123_NEUTERED = true`, which restores the pre-T123 360px fixed cap and is the reported symptom exactly. Two `columnWidths` tests at 1.0/1.25/1.5/2.0 pin the same property purely - sum of columns plus gaps equals the available width, and the wide column takes more than 90% of it. Filed D73 for the judgement call: a parity task whose fix landed in an unversioned user-config script outside this repo.
- 2026-08-12: T739 - a pane that reconnects to its background session now writes down the position its session actually reached, so the NEXT reconnect replays everything the program printed in between instead of skipping it. `Remote.appliedOffset()` is what the manifest persists as the next attach's resume point, and it counted every byte fed to the parser - including the two things the agent INJECTS on attach that are not the session's stream at all: its `[N bytes of scrollback lost]` marker and its `grid_snapshot` repaint of the visible screen. So every re-attach recorded a point past the agent's own head by exactly the repaint's size (197 bytes, measured), the next attach was clamped back to the head (T532), and whatever real output sat between the two was never replayed. Invisible on a quiet pane, because the repaint covers the same screen; silently lost output on a busy one. The proposal in the task - "a frame anchored at or below where we already are does not advance us" - cannot work, and that is the interesting part: the repaint is anchored at the head S and so is the first LIVE frame after it, identical on the wire, so only the sender can say which is which. The agent therefore frames its injections as `DATA_REPAINT` (0x15, same `DataPayload`), gated on a new `repaint_data` capability for the reason `open_failed`/`attach_failed` are gated - an unknown opcode is a fatal framing error - and the client tracks position by ANCHOR rather than by counting (`Pane.stream_pos`, advanced by the pure `streamPosAfter`, adopted in `drainRing` when a pre-pop read is followed by an empty pop, which proves every byte handed over is parsed). That second half fixes the evicted-scrollback case for free: the position jumps the hole instead of counting bytes across it. Validating it found a second defect that nothing else could have: a new data-lane opcode was SILENTLY SWALLOWED, because both muxes fold one transport back into two lanes with `frame.type == .data`, so `DATA_REPAINT` went to the CONTROL lane where the control reader ignores what it does not recognize - the agent sent a 197-byte snapshot, the client had negotiated it, and nothing arrived, with no crash and no log. The fold is one shared predicate now (`protocol.onDataLane`), used by `client_mux`, the agent's `mux` and the mock that exists to mirror the rule. New `test\win32\session-resume-offset.ps1` (ALL PASS, 68 assertions): three kill/restore cycles where `requested == head` exactly, with `GHOZTTY_RESUME_COUNT_BYTES=1` as teeth (the pre-T739 accounting, from the same tree, overshoots and gets clamped on every cycle after the first) and a suppressed-capability arm for skew. `session-persistence.ps1` section D now runs a SECOND flood cycle, which is the one whose resume point the previous attach wrote. Filed T803 (the Mac seat's measurement) and T804 (the cross-machine case, where nothing repaints behind the injection and the framing is what saves it).

- 2026-08-12: T773 - the "freshly built binary bakes a stale commit stamp" is a MISREAD, and the misread is what got fixed. `+version` answers for two binaries: its own `Version` block, and a `Running Instance` block describing whatever app is running, fetched over IPC (T52) - and that second block owns the only line literally labelled `commit`. The P1's evidence read it, which is also why a Debug build and a ReleaseFast build "agreed" on a 12-hours-old sha: both probes had dialed the same installed release the 05:17 refresh delivered. Measured live at HEAD `66ad87d45`: one document, `- version: ...+66ad87d45` (this binary, == HEAD) above `- commit  : 445780e49` (the running app, pid 50828); `Resolve-GhozttyExeCommit` returns `66ad87d45` and `Test-CommitsMatch` against HEAD is `True`, so every delivery gate was reading the right number throughout and `launch-upgrade.ps1` would not have refused. The agent's stamp was not stale either, for an unrelated reason: `GhosttyAgent.versionString` deliberately stamps the last commit touching the AGENT's compiled sources, not HEAD, so app and agent disagreeing is the design (a HEAD-derived stamp used to make every release look like a newer agent and prompt users to reset live sessions for an identical binary). What was genuinely wrong: the separation between the two blocks is ONE SPACE (`version:` vs `version :`) and no test held it. `test\win32\upgrade-staleness.ps1` gains A31-A35, a payload in that day's shape whose two blocks name DIFFERENT commits - teeth-checked by relaxing the anchor to `version\s*:`, which turns A33 and A34 red and nothing else - plus B11-B13, which make the freeze checkable instead of assumed (the exact `git log` line `GitVersion.detect` bakes must name HEAD; the exe's stamp must be a real commit object reachable from HEAD). The artifact-level form is deliberately not asserted and the script says why: an mtime cannot tell "built from an older tree" from "the tree moved under a good binary", and both seats push here, so it would fabricate failures (T197). `Invoke-GhozttyVersionText` now bounds the running-app query at `GHOZTTY_IPC_TIMEOUT_MS=2000` - reading a FILE's identity had a hard dependency on an unrelated app answering inside the probe's 20s deadline while T755's default is 30s, so a busy app could turn "read this binary's stamp" into "the delivery cannot verify itself". ALL PASS: upgrade-staleness (101), upgrade-no-fork (128), deliver-windows-build, morning-refresh, build-mode-guard, ipc-version. Filed T805 (make `+version` self-disambiguating on both platforms, since the misreading is a real UX defect in the output).

- 2026-08-12: T744 - every launch in the acceptance suite now states what it wants session persistence to do, so the audit that checks it is green and a future red run means a NEW mistake rather than this old one. Five sites were undeclared, not the four the task was filed for: `session-resume-offset.ps1:255` arrived with T739 in the day between filing and repair, which is this defect's own shape - the property regrows at roughly the rate new acceptance scripts land, and nothing runs the sweep between times (evidence noted onto T777, whose premise this is; the aggregate entry point is T732). Each site was fixed by STATING intent, never by widening what the sweep accepts, and the intent differs per site: `agent-attach-refused.ps1:276` and `session-resume-offset.ps1:255` want persistence ON and say so, because one restores the manifest the section above it wrote and the other WRITES the manifest every restore cycle below it reads back - the flag there would delete the fixture, not isolate the test. The three `url-scheme.ps1` activations (359/368/381) are the marker's own named exemption: `runUrlSchemeActivation` answers and exits before the single-instance bind (`src/main_ghostty.zig:86`, T695), so an activation opens no terminal and never reaches the restore path at all. Each of the three needs its own marker because the lookback is six lines per site, which is the rule working rather than a limitation. Measured: `Get-GhozttyLaunchSites` reports `total=186 undeclared=0`; ALL PASS: persistence-flag (20), url-scheme (32), agent-attach-refused (24), session-resume-offset (68), P1 (25), P2 (20), P3 (16); floor lanes none/win32/agent all PASS.
- 2026-08-12: T783 - an acceptance harness that nobody ran now says so, instead of sitting quietly red. `b64c3e8aa` prefixed every `scripts\go-loop-lock.ps1` message with an ISO timestamp; 26 assertions in `test\win32\go-loop-guard.ps1` anchor on the answer's first word (`^ACQUIRED`, `^held`, `^stale-dead`), so the loop's own harness was red for a day against a lock script that was working perfectly - it is not in the P1-P3 floor and nothing tied a `scripts\go-loop-*.ps1` edit to it. `scripts\guard-due.ps1` answers "has anybody run harness X against the code as it now stands?" from a COMMITTED stamp: a coverage table maps a harness to the files it is about (the `go-loop` row covers `scripts\go-loop-*.ps1`, `scripts\loop-session.ps1` and the harness itself), a clean green run stamps the SHA-256 of each, and `check` reports `GUARD CURRENT` or `GUARD DUE` naming every file that changed, appeared or vanished. Four properties it was built for: it is a CHANGE gate, so a file edited and edited back is not due and a stamp never goes stale with time; hashing folds CRLF and strips a BOM, because `.ps1` carries no `text` attribute in `.gitattributes` and a raw hash would report every file as changed on a differently-configured clone; the stamp is committed, so a `git pull` carrying another seat's loop-script edit reads as DUE here, which no local mtime check can see; and only a CLEAN green run stamps - red stays due, and a run with skipped sections prints `stamp NOT updated` rather than certifying code it did not measure. Two wirings, deliberately unequal in force: `go-loop-exec.ps1 claim` (go.md step 0) REPORTS and can never fail, because a claim that exits nonzero over a stale stamp would wedge the loop, which is the disease and not the cure; `parity-tasks.ps1 validate` (step 6, before every commit) FAILS, with a `-NoGuardDue` hatch that prints that it was used. `-TaskDir` given by a caller means a fixture run and is not gated - a distinction that needs `$TaskDirGiven` captured before the default fills the parameter in. Measured end to end on the real repo, in order: `guard-due check` DUE naming `scripts/go-loop-exec.ps1` + `test/win32/go-loop-guard.ps1` -> `go-loop-guard.ps1` ALL PASS + `STAMPED go-loop (7 files)` -> `GUARD CURRENT go-loop (7 files, stamped 2026-08-12 from 8f94d28c8)` -> `validate` ALL PASS (835 tasks). ALL PASS: guard-due (34 assertions, whose sections D and E measure the two forces against each other against a deliberately-DUE fixture repo), go-loop-guard, P1 (25), P2 (20), P3 (16); floor lanes none/win32/agent all PASS. Filed T806 for the rest of the table - every harness outside the floor still has this gap, and adding a row is the whole cost of closing it.

- 2026-08-12: T460 - a crash now yields its stack on the FIRST occurrence, with no re-run. T450's capture re-runs the crashed binary under cdb, which can only ever describe a crash that agrees to happen twice - and the crash it was built for lands on about half of runs, so the occurrence that actually failed the lane was precisely the one it could not see (D6, user: "identify ways to find crash details faster... we want it to be easy to diagnose crashes so that we can capture and fix them faster"). Nothing needed inventing, which is the finding: measured on this box, WER's LocalDumps is already enabled machine-wide, and a zig Debug binary that dies already leaves a minidump in `%LOCALAPPDATA%\CrashDumps` at the moment it dies - unattended, on the first crash, at zero cost to a run that does not crash - and nothing read it. `cdb -z` of that dump yields exactly what the re-run yields: every thread, the faulting frame (`avthread!boom`) sitting BELOW zig's `handleSegfaultWindows` so the handler's own abort does not destroy it, and source lines - in about a second instead of ~10 minutes. So the fix is a reader (`scripts\lib\CrashDump.ps1`), not a new capture mechanism: `floor-lane.ps1` reads the dump first and reaches the re-run only when there is none, and `crash-catch.ps1` gained `-Last`/`-FromDump` (read a crash that already happened) and `-Status` (is this box armed at all). Three measured facts the design turns on. LocalDumps is HKLM-only - an HKCU key with a DumpFolder was ignored outright and the dump still went to the HKLM default - so a full-memory `DumpType=2` needs elevation and is an upgrade, not a precondition; the default mini dump already carries every thread's stack, which is what a stack question needs. The recorded exception is `0x80000003`, zig's handler aborting, NOT the access violation, so the block says so rather than leaving a reader chasing a breakpoint that never existed. And whether a dump is a crash at all is asked of the FILE, not of cdb: cdb reports `80000003 (Break instruction exception)` off the current context for a dump holding no exception - indistinguishable in its output from a real abort - so a T48 freeze-watchdog dump of a healthy process would have read as a crash and manufactured a stack for a bug that never happened; `Test-MinidumpHasException` reads the stream directory for an ExceptionStream instead. A dump older than the run that is asking is never returned, for the same reason: a wrong stack costs more than no stack. Acceptance `test\win32\crash-first-chance.ps1` ALL PASS (49 assertions, 0 skipped), whose lane arm drives a crasher through the new `floor-lane.ps1 -Command` and requires BOTH directions - the dump path when a dump exists, and, under `GHOZTTY_CRASH_NO_WER=1` (a box with no capture, reproduced from this same tree), the re-run fallback, so "the lane did not re-run" is falsifiable rather than merely observed. Also ALL PASS: crash-stacks (the T450 path untouched), crash-diagnostics, P1-P3; floor lanes none/win32/agent all PASS. Added a `crash-first-chance` row to the T783 guard table so this machinery cannot go quietly red - and adding it broke eight arms of guard-due's own fixture-based harness, which is fixed in the MECHANISM rather than in the test: a row covering no file in the target tree is now `GUARD N/A`, not DUE, since there is nothing there that could have changed. That is what T806 needs before it can add rows en masse. Filed T807 (SkipAudit never examines a scorer verdict line that carries no string literal, so a correct `Write-TestVerdict -Skipped` cannot credit the count on its own), T808 (an elevated one-time arm for full-memory dumps) and T809 (nothing yet reads the APP's own first-crash dump when a GUI acceptance script kills it).
- 2026-08-12: T461 - selecting a remote machine in the chooser now dials it ONCE, and everything about that machine rides the same connection. Every roster fetch of a remote row used to dial the relay, run LIST_SESSIONS and free the connection again, so N refetches cost N WebSocket upgrades and N relay authentications - and, the part that blocks the features stacked on top, there was nowhere to hang anything that has to keep LISTENING (T462's per-session CPU meter needs a connection that outlives one RPC, which a dial-read-free probe cannot host by construction). `App.machine_pool` is the remote-side counterpart to `LocalAgent`'s warm connection and the win32 half of Mac's `MachineConnectionPool.swift` (60ccd4f45). The rules are pure and in the `none` lane - `src/apprt/win32/machine_pool.zig`: keying by ENDPOINT (`relay:<base>|<device>` / `tcp:<host>:<port>`, so two rows naming one device share one socket, and a rotated token is the same machine but is still refreshed on every acquire), the lease refcount (dial on first borrow, free on the LAST release, an inert release for a machine nobody holds), a pool-wide monotonic generation so a dial that lands after its machine was released, invalidated or re-dialed is FREED rather than installed, and a 5s cooldown so a refetch storm cannot become a dial storm. The resources are `MachineConnectionPool.zig`: a detached dial posting `WM_APP+28`, link-state and warm-replay notifications on `WM_APP+27` carrying integers only (a link callback runs on the connection's own reader thread, which may not allocate GUI state or re-enter `Connection`), and an atomically refcounted `Entry` - the pool holds one reference, every borrow holds another - which is Mac's ARC retain in win32 dress and is what makes the invalidation path safe with no synchronous delivery: a borrow the "stop using this" notification has not reached yet is holding the transport up by construction. Only a DEAD link invalidates (the FSM enters `reconnecting` on a few missed heartbeats and snaps back on the next authentic packet - `agent_recovery.settle_ms`'s reasoning, minus the settle window, because nothing here rebuilds windows). `SessionRoster`'s worker lost its relay dial and its whole `OwnedRemote` deep-copy; a remote fetch borrows or does nothing, and the `unauthorized` verdict moved to the pool while the roster keeps printing the same `fetch failed ... state=...` sentence, which is what the suite reads. TWO LIFETIME BUGS found on the way, both fixed here: `MachineChooser.close` - the REAL teardown path - never called `roster.deinit()`, so every chooser dismissal leaked the fetched sessions and the parsed layout manifest (only `destroyState`, the early returns in `open`, did); and that same divergence left the pool lease behind, whose callback context is the chooser, so the SECOND chooser's dial notified the first chooser's ghost and the app died at `0xffffffffffffffff` - caught by the new acceptance script on its first run, which is exactly the "crashes far from the cause" the Mac counterpart's comment warns about. Both paths now go through one `releaseOwned`. New acceptance `test\win32\chooser-conn-pool.ps1` ALL PASS (19), whose oracle is the FAKE RELAY's own request log rather than the app's account of itself: five refetches of one machine, zero further connects, paired with the app's load count because one dial only means something if the fetches ran, plus the chooser's close dropping the connection and a second chooser re-dialing as the control that the pool did not simply stop dialing. T328's Kill re-measured over the pooled connection: `chooser-sessions-remote.ps1` ALL PASS (20) and its `-NegativeControl` arm (13). Neighbours green: chooser-roster-refetch (8), chooser-sessions (17), chooser-restore-all-remote (40), persistence-flag (20), plus the five harness sweeps. Floor: none/win32/agent PASS, P1-P3 ALL PASS (25/20/16). `chooser-resume.ps1` is red at its own setup, pre-existing and already filed as T793. Filed T810 (the Activity Monitor and Restore All still dial their own per-machine connections) and T811 - the agent lane's FIRST run of this turn died after 9432/9512 tests with a DebugAllocator panic inside `Connection.destroy` at the end of T739's repaint test, an intermittent this turn's diff cannot reach (win32 apprt only) and which the identical lane passed on the next run; T460's first-chance dump captured the faulting thread, so the task carries a stack instead of a suspicion.

- 2026-08-12: T467 - the audit of every win32 window class for the redraw bug T456 found in one of them. `CS_HREDRAW | CS_VREDRAW` is what makes Windows invalidate the WHOLE client on a resize instead of only the strip the resize uncovered, and it is a property of the class, set once at registration. Twenty-four registration sites: twenty classes in the app, the agent's never-shown tray window, three test-only parents. Four answered yes and lacked it, all the same shape as the banner - owner-painted, laid out against their own bounds, and returning 1 from `WM_ERASEBKGND` so the stale pixels are not even erased. `ActivityMonitor` is the one that mattered: it is the only panel here the USER resizes by dragging its frame, every element of it is measured from the client rect `layout()` reads back, and `WM_SIZE` only re-places the child controls - so a drag left the whole owner-painted table drawn at the width it used to have. `GhozttyViewerNav` (right-anchored buttons, address field spanning the rest) and `GhozttyViewerFeedback` (pill, carousel and send row placed from width) are resized on every bounds sync with `MoveWindow(.., TRUE)`, which paints what is invalid without making more of it invalid. `GhozttyViewerTOC` survived in practice for an accidental reason worth writing down: `place()` calls `SetWindowRgn(.., TRUE)` right after its `MoveWindow` and that redraws - a side effect, not a contract, and the gutter branch passes a null region. Three of the task's own named suspects answered NO, against the filed suspicion: `Scrollbar`, `KeyStateIndicator` and `ReadonlyBadge` never receive `WM_PAINT` at all - they are `WS_EX_LAYERED` windows painted by `UpdateLayeredWindow`, i.e. push-model, where the class style is inert. The scrollbar thumb IS a function of the track height, as filed; it is simply repainted rather than invalidated, and every resize path calls `repaint()`. The rest are no for stated reasons (flat fill; the top-level window invalidating its caption band and tab strip by hand and deliberately, so a resize does not repaint the child-covered pane area; the renderer redrawing the terminal surface whole every frame; fixed-size `WS_POPUP` dialogs with no `WS_THICKFRAME`, no `WM_SIZE` and no self-resize). The audit table is the deliverable and lives in `docs/design/win32-design-system.md` section 5c, where the next window class will be added, not in the task file. Asserted by a shared probe, `src/apprt/win32/class_redraw.zig`: a real window of the class, on-screen at layered alpha 0 (T456's trap - parked off-monitor it has an empty visible region, Windows invalidates nothing, and the assertion passes for the wrong reason), resized along ONE axis at a time so a class carrying a single style bit cannot pass, reading `GetUpdateRect` back. It registers its own positive and negative control classes, identical but for the style bits, so every run re-proves the probe can tell them apart instead of leaving that to an experiment somebody remembers running. Teeth measured directly: rebuilt with `ActivityMonitor` at `.style = 0`, the lane reports `width resize invalidated 40x200 of a 440x200 client` and the test fails; restored, it passes. Floor: none/win32/agent all PASS via `floor-lane.ps1 -Lane all`; P1-P3 ALL PASS. Filed T819 (the command palette and search popups ride the terminal's own class, so they cannot take the style without giving it to every terminal surface - they only resize on a DPI change while open) and D75 (a large uncommitted `CLAUDE.md` to `docs/claude/` refactor was already in the working tree when this turn claimed the loop, with seven untracked files and a dozen rewritten cross-references; it was left entirely untouched and only this task's own paths were committed, which is why the audit went into the tracked rulebook rather than the untracked `docs/claude/win32-ui.md`).
- 2026-08-12: T471 - a remote pane's scrollback guard now follows the CHILD's pty, not the window's OS. T431's guard (`src/termio/history_guard.zig`) switched itself on with `builtin.os.tag == .windows`, which answers "does the LOCAL machine run ConPTY children" - the same question for a local pane, the wrong one for a cross-OS remote pane. A Mac window on a Windows agent owned a ConPTY child with the guard compiled out and lost history on every grow (the half that was real data loss); a Windows window on a POSIX agent armed a guard it did not need. The flavour now rides the HELLO as `Hello.pty_flavor` (`protocol.PtyFlavor`, `conpty`/`posix`), an additive optional FIELD with no capability gate - it opens no opcode and re-means no existing value, the same class as `hostname`/`build_version`, which the module's compatibility history now states as a rule rather than leaving as three precedents. The agent advertises what it really spawns, `connection.zig` captures `peer_pty_flavor` during negotiation, `termio.Remote` caches it once the pane is live (IO thread writes it, IO thread resizes, so no synchronization), and `history_guard.enabled` became `enabledFor(?PtyFlavor)` asked per pane through `backend.childPtyFlavor()`. Null - an older agent, or a spelling this build never heard of - falls back to `local_flavor`, bit-for-bit the pre-T471 answer, so skew is an unimproved case and never a regression. macOS needs no Swift change: the guard is shared core, so both directions are fixed by one commit. The measurement problem was that the behaviour needs two machines and two operating systems, so `GHOZTTY_AGENT_PTY_FLAVOR` (Debug/ReleaseSafe only, same shape as `protoVersionOverride`) lets one box answer as the other: `test\win32\history-guard-flavor.ps1` fills 500 numbered lines into an agent-backed pane and grows it, twice. Truthful agent - 0 lost. Agent reporting `posix` over the same real ConPTY child - 18 lost, lines 459-476, exactly the rows the taller viewport gained and exactly T431's signature. That LOSS is the assertion: a client still deciding from `builtin.os.tag` comes back clean there, so it is what makes the field load-bearing, and it can only pass through a real HELLO (an exec pane reports this machine's flavour and loses nothing). Floor: none/win32/agent PASS, P1-P3 ALL PASS, `scrollback-narrow.ps1` ALL PASS (no regression to the local path), and the six harness audits clean with the new script in the tree. Filed T821 (the Mac-seat half - a Mac window on a Windows agent, watched by someone sitting in front of it) and T822 (the CLAUDE.md progressive-disclosure split found sitting uncommitted in the working tree, owned by no task).

- 2026-08-14: T472 - a remote-connection test waits on a wall clock now, so a busy box cannot manufacture a timeout. Five waits in `src/remote/connection.zig`'s tests gave up after a fixed number of fruitless yields, and a spin count does not measure time, it measures scheduler contention: on a box running three test lanes and a WebView2 host, 100_000 yields can burn through in far less time than the writer thread needs, so a green tree produced `error.Timeout` at random. `TestDeadline` replaces all five (`drainChannel`, `spinUntil`, the two T739 `streamPos` waits, the metrics-unsub wait) with a ten-second budget - generous on purpose, an upper bound on a hang rather than a performance assertion - and its unit test asserts both directions, the second being the property the old oracle lacked: 200_000 yields against a ten-minute budget still has not expired. A `drainChannel` timeout now prints the budget, how many of the wanted bytes arrived and what they were, so a red run is readable without a debugger. Fault (2) of the report - the timeout laundered into a panic at `destroy`'s `assert(writer_thread == null)` - needed no code: T693 already made `destroy` call `shutdown` when `threadsLive()`, covered by its own test, so it was verified rather than rebuilt. Measured: `-Lane win32 -Repeat 5` 5/5 PASS, `none` PASS, P1/P2/P3 ALL PASS (25/20/16), and the reported failure mode did not recur in 20 lane runs. **The turn's real find is elsewhere: T443's armed watch fired, five times.** Three agent-lane and two win32-lane runs aborted in `terminal.PageList` (x2), `terminal.Screen`, `terminal.formatter` and `font.Collection` - four of the five `Page.assertIntegrity` reporting a corrupted page-map metadata pointer, the fifth the FreeType heap - none of them reachable from this diff, which an A/B settles (connection.zig at its HEAD content 3/3 PASS, the edit restored 3/3 PASS, same quiesced box). Both halves are in T443's ARMED-WATCH LOG with the fact that matters most: **5 aborts in 21 lane runs today against a baseline of 190+ crash-free runs**, i.e. the rate has changed by orders of magnitude and the corrupter is finally cheap to hunt - `scripts\crash-databreak.ps1` now has a ~1-in-3 chance per armed run, and the agent lane alone is 3 of 5. T443 is back to `todo` at P0/order 9 per its own unblock protocol. Filed T831 (one shared wall-clock test-wait helper plus a sweep for the spin-count oracles that are left - `src/remote/agent/pty_child.zig` had independently arrived at the same answer for the same reason under T89b, and nothing stops the third from being a spin count again).
- 2026-08-14: T443 - the corruption hunt has a reproducible condition at last, and it is the zig build runner. Every soak this task ever cited ran the test binary directly out of `.zig-cache`, and that is a condition the crash has never once occurred in: the exact `ghoztty-agent-core-test.exe` that had already aborted three times this morning ran 12 times at 4-way concurrency without a fault, against 5 aborts in 26 lane runs the same day. Cumulatively the file holds ~200 standalone runs with zero crashes against a ~19% per-run rate under `zig build`, i.e. `0.81^200`, so "it will not reproduce" was never a property of the defect - it was a property of the harness. `zig build` passes `--listen=-`, so `lib/compiler/test_runner.zig` takes `mainServer()` and drives one test per pipe message instead of running them back to back off one stack frame; `scripts\test-binary-soak.ps1` and `scripts\crash-databreak.ps1` both take the other path, so the instrument built to catch the write in the act would have sat armed forever. Filed as T832. The damage is pinned to the byte for the first time too, because `210c763f4`'s diagnostic finally fired: `ptr=0x11a60cb29de28 page_base=0x1c9cb22f000 page_len=0x6f000`, whose low 32 bits are `base + 0x6ee28` exactly while the high half went `0x1c9 -> 0x11a60`. A `u32` offset added to a base can carry the high half by at most one, so the addition did not produce that pointer - and disassembling `OffsetHashMap.map` IN the crashing binary shows a zero-extended offset, a full 64-bit `add` and a full 8-byte store through the sret, with the caller reloading all 8 bytes. That retires the 2026-08-04 reading (a truncation across `get` -> `getContext` -> `getAdapted`): the pointer is already wrong when `map()` returns, which means `Page.memory.ptr` as loaded at that call site was already half-clobbered while another copy of it in the same stack frame was intact, and the target moves up a level to a 4-byte write on a base-pointer copy. Landed with the analysis: `Page.mapPtrDamage` classifies a bad map pointer as `exact` / `low_half_only` / `neither`, and `assertMapPtrInPage` now prints the map offset, the pointer the arithmetic should have produced and that verdict, so the next occurrence answers "was the base wrong or the product?" without a debugger - unit tested against the dump's verbatim values. Floor: `floor-lane.ps1 -Lane all` ALL LANES PASS, `-Lane agent -Repeat 5` PASS x5, P1/P2/P3 ALL PASS.


- 2026-08-14: T832 - the two instruments built to catch T443's corruption now run the tests the way that makes them crash, and say so when they do not. Both of them took a binary out of `.zig-cache\o` and ran it directly, which is a condition the defect has never once occurred in: ~200 standalone runs across T443 with zero crashes - including the exact `ghoztty-agent-core-test.exe` that had dumped three times that morning - against 5 aborts in 26 `zig build` lane runs the same day. `zig build` passes `--listen=-`, so `lib/compiler/test_runner.zig` takes `mainServer()` and drives one test per pipe message instead of running them back to back off one stack frame. So a soak could report all-clear indefinitely, and an armed data breakpoint would have sat there for its 10-30 minutes catching nothing, forever. `test-binary-soak.ps1` gained `-Mode auto|build-runner|standalone`, defaulting to the build runner whenever a `-Lane` is named; a round is one `zig build <lane>` driven through `floor-lane.ps1`, so it inherits that script's CPU/stall watchdog and crash capture rather than growing a second copy of both, and rounds never overlap (T401). Each round is classified from floor-lane's exit code plus a crash scan of the LANE log, and the summary now leads with `mode=`. The crash-pattern list gained `thread \d+ panic:`, because four of the five 2026-08-14 aborts were Zig panics rather than faults and a fault-only list filed this task's own signal as a red test. `crash-databreak.ps1` gained the same default: it starts the lane detached, waits for the build runner to launch a test binary, and ATTACHES cdb to it, reading the image path off the RUNNING process so a rebuild or a `-Filter` cannot leave it armed against a binary nobody is running. Following children (`cdb -o`) was tried first and cannot work here, for two measured reasons now written into the code: `g` returns once per child attach, so a script ending `g; q` quits at the first one and reports `0 arm cycles, exit 0` - indistinguishable from a clean run; and `bu <module>+<rva>` is rejected outright ("Bp expression contains symbols not qualified with module name") because cdb reads a bare module name as a symbol. Measured end to end: `-Lane agent -Runs 5` = five real `zig build test-agent` rounds, `mode=build-runner runs=5 pass=5 crash=0`; `-Lane none -Filter terminal.Screen -Symbol assertIntegrity` attached to the `ghostty-test.exe` the build runner started and reported **84,356 arm cycles / 84,356 disarms over 193s, exit 0**. New acceptance `test\win32\test-binary-soak.ps1` ALL PASS (22 assertions), whose build-runner arms are staged through `floor-lane.ps1 -Command` so the CRASH classification is proven against the exact 2026-08-14 abort text rather than waiting for a real one; `test\win32\crash-databreak.ps1` ALL PASS with a new section that starts a fixture independently and proves the attach path still catches a staged wild write with writer, victim frame and dump. Both are now rows in `guard-due.ps1`, which is what keeps this from decaying - an instrument that has quietly stopped measuring is indistinguishable from good news, which is the whole defect. Floor: `floor-lane.ps1 -Lane all` ALL LANES PASS (none 287s / win32 344s / agent 186s), P1/P2/P3 ALL PASS (25/20/16). Filed **T834**: the first real armed attempt at T443's actual target attached correctly and then refused at the probe - `Page.verifyIntegrity`'s frame is now `0x1020` bytes, so zig emits a `__chkstk` prologue with two extra pushes and `Invoke-DataBreakProbe` only knows the small-frame shape, a growth caused by this hunt's own diagnostics. T443 now depends on T834 rather than sitting at the head of the queue behind a step it cannot take. Also logged onto T443: the first honest build-runner rate measurement, 0 crashes in 5 agent-lane rounds this afternoon against 3-in-5 the same morning, so the rate is unstable within the condition too.
- 2026-08-14: T833 - unfolding a collapsed banner repaints now, instead of leaving a stale half-open card in a full-height band. User report, 2026-08-14: collapse a multi-line banner, expand it, and the card stays unpainted. It reproduced on a build carrying HEAD's behavior, and the measurement is the clearest statement of the defect: over the whole expand the card was painted at `68, 68` - the COLLAPSED height - inside the 160px band the layout had already reserved, while the T149 animation heartbeat logged all eleven frames it wanted to draw. The two halves had never been the same thing. `onCollapseTick` re-glues the popup and calls `updatePosition`, which repaints only when the WINDOW's size changed; collapsing, the popup shrinks with the card, so every frame invalidated for free (CS_HREDRAW|CS_VREDRAW, T467) and the direction looked correct. Expanding, the toggle relayouts the grid ONCE to the settled taller band - deliberately, so the terminal grid is not dragged through eleven resizes (T149, Mac 89465f320) - so the window reaches its final size before the first animated frame and never changes again. Nothing dirtied the client after that, and the card froze on whichever frame the toggle's own `InvalidateRect` happened to catch. The tick now dirties the client itself, keyed on the height that was actually PAINTED rather than the one the last tick wanted (so a frame that rounds to the same height still has nothing to draw, which is the property the resize path had for free), and finishes the frame with `UpdateWindow` in the same tick instead of a pumped WM_PAINT later - T456's reasoning, one direction over. The test gap underneath was that `banner collapse h=` is written by the heartbeat, so it proves what the animation intended and nothing about what reached the screen; `pane-banner.ps1` asserted the intended frames and passed throughout. Paint now logs `banner paint h=` from inside `paint`, section 6f2 asserts the painted frames in both directions, and a win32-lane unit test asserts the painted height moving while the window height holds still. Both negative controls are honest: `T833_NEUTERED` fails exactly the two expand assertions in the script (2 FAILURE(S), 121 passed) and the new unit test. Full script ALL PASS (123), floor all three lanes PASS. One thing found while validating and NOT fixed here: T745's table-width probe in the same script is nondeterministic - the same banner renders its long value at the full content column most of the time and at 55-85% of it otherwise, measured 3 wrong in 8 renders on a FIXED build and 3 in 8 on a neutered one, so it predates this work. That is the user's own 2026-08-11 screenshot symptom surviving intermittently, and it is filed as T835 (P0) with the repro recipe; `pane-banner.ps1` currently goes red about one run in three because of it.

- 2026-08-14: T834 - the instrument built to catch the T443 corruption can aim at its target again. `Invoke-DataBreakProbe` read exactly one prologue shape (`push rbp` / `sub rsp,X` / `lea rbp,[rsp+Y]`) and refused `Page.verifyIntegrity`, because this hunt's own diagnostics had grown that frame to `0x1020` bytes - past 4 KB the compiler allocates the frame with a `__chkstk` stack probe and saves two more registers first. The prologue walk is now a cursor rather than fixed indices: `push rbp`, then any run of callee-saved pushes, then EITHER `sub rsp,X` or `mov eax,X; call __chkstk; sub rsp,rax`, then the `lea`. Those pushes are not cosmetic - each one moves the return-address slot 8 bytes further from `rbp`, and that slot is where the one-shot disarm breakpoint goes, so miscounting them would leave every armed slot live after the function returned; the math generalises to `ret = rbp + 8 + 8*pushes + X - Y`. The acceptance fixture needed a second ingredient nobody would guess: a >4 KB frame produces the `__chkstk` allocation on its own but NOT the `push rsi`/`push rdi` pair (measured at 0x1690 and 0x2c70 bytes, both `ExtraPushes = 0`), so it forces them with an inline-asm rsi/rdi clobber and reproduces the seven-instruction prologue exactly. Proven rather than asserted: the fixture arms and DISARMS 40 of 40 calls, which can only happen if the computed return slot is right, and the real thing then ran - `crash-databreak.ps1 -Lane agent -Symbol verifyIntegrity -SignatureFilter page.Page` armed `@rbp+0x4d8/+0x4e0/+0x4e8` on the live `ghoztty_agent_core_test!verifyIntegrity` and turned over **335,878 arm cycles with 335,878 disarms** before its 20-minute clock ran out. That timeout is the one thing to be careful with and it is filed as T836: the verdict line a reader would quote reads `no wild write observed` whether the program finished or the tool killed it, and here it did not finish - at ~2 ms per armed call the instrument is now the bottleneck, so the next armed hunt needs a much longer window or a narrower arm, and must not read a clock as an all-clear. `test\win32\crash-databreak.ps1` ALL PASS (62 checks, 13 new; the small-frame sections green and now asserting `FrameShape = sub` explicitly); floor lanes none/win32/agent PASS, P1 (25) / P2 (20) / P3 (16) ALL PASS. T474 and T443 were both waiting on this and are unblocked. One thing seen while running the floor and NOT explained here: the agent lane reported `PASS in 191s` and stopped writing its log at 14:15:20, yet both of its test binaries were still alive at 14:40 with their CPU frozen at ~122s - a leak, possibly a wedge at exit, filed with the numbers as T837.
